An addictive restaurant management sim that's polished enough to hold interest, particularly if you enjoy the core gameplay loop of gathering ingredients, choosing what dishes to serve and making dishes to order. If you're a Touhou fan I expect you may get a bit more out of the story than I did as there is more dialogue than you might expect at first glance. I played mainly on Steam Deck which felt perfect for running a few nights of the izakaya while watching tv or on a break. Progress synced well enough that I could pick up on PC at other times without any worry. I really liked some of the art (particularly of all the different dishes!) and the music was pleasant, but may get a bit repetitive if you spend hours playing at a time. Very enjoyable if you're into casual management sims, and while it's sometimes a little rough around the edges I didn't notice any real bugs while playing. If you don't read Chinese make sure that any DLC you buy has an English release as they usually release in Chinese first - unless you want to muddle through in which case go for it! Dialogue may seem slightly wonky to English speakers but is plenty good enough to understand.Mainly focused around daytime gathering and talking to NPCs/buying from vendors, then running the izakaya at night. Daytime tasks are time-management focused with most actions taking 30 minutes. NPCs will give you tasks to complete which will reward you with new recipes or other useful upgrades (and story!). The izakaya management revolves around upgrading your locations/cooking tools, and serving endless streams of customers with a little cooking mini-game. You will eventually unlock things that make the day-time foraging and talking to people more efficient so you can focus on running the izakaya at night, but some of it is not very well signposted (at least in the English translation) so a guide can be helpful at times. There is also a main overarching story to complete, so the game is not endless (unless you want it to be..)There are a fair amount of achievements you will get simply for playing the game. There was one where I needed to know in advance I would reload and make a different decision on a specific day, so if you're hunting for 100% completion you will want to look some of them up beforehand or risk having to replay if you don't have a save file from near that decision. Most are simply a case of playing long enough - I got to 100% achievement completion in about 80 hours but if you're more efficient you could definitely get there sooner. At the time of review I only own the base game and DLC1 so I can't comment on later DLCs.

game: Cell to Singularity - Evolution Never Ends
text: Cell to Singularity (CtS) is probably one of the best idle / clicker games out there. Having a backing of real science and learning is actually a cool benefit. I've actually learned a few things along that way, and I think that's a pretty cool bonus. PresentationCts is very simply designed in the beginning and everything feels intuitive. As you progress through the primary simulation, more things unlock, per usual, and more features and functions are added. Progression also rewards two more simulations which are somewhat connected to the primary. It's a way of breaking up the game play and keeping things interesting. The Primary and Beyond sims feel well laid out, but the Dino sim feels messy, but that could be by design based on the era and motif presented. ProgressionProgression feels consistent across all sims. There's only a light amount of grinding in most areas, and generally things move along well when idling as well. The biggest problem I encountered were when I didn't get silver or gold tier cards in the Dino and Beyond sims. This caused some stagnation and after getting most of the badges, there's still a few cards I don't have. RNG can ruin the fun a little.Does The Game Feel Good?For an idle / clicker game to feel good, it has to reward progression. Progression is a fine balance of systems which some devs get really wrong and some get really right. I feel like CtS has a good feeling of progression and rewards as you flow through the different sims accelerates. Final Verdict9 / 10. Enjoyable, rewarding, and not overly grindy. Every clicker / idler has some form of grind, but sometimes the grind is just too much. I think CtS strikes a good balance. Other than some end game nit picks (Alpha Centauri just takes to long to max out for the badge), I think it was well done.

The game started out all good and well. The party-based combat is pretty standard for turn-based tactical RPGs. Class progression is fairly open. You can pick talents from any of the three subclass trees in the character's class, so that kind of leaves some room for specialization. The story is enjoyable for the most part and keeps things going at a steady pace for the first 6-8 hours. But then it just grinds to a halt and you have to just sit there and "conquer" a dozen territories at a snail's pace via the army battle system. It's not like the enemies are difficult to defeat or you need to prepare some kind of grand strategy. It's basically 1) have the bigger number and 2) select the option that balances your army stats throughout the battle. Easy. The loot rewards at the end of each battle is demoralizingly plain as well. The game literally just becomes: click on red border region, watch horse glide there, find enemy settlement, click attack button, wait until army gets there, do the battle thing, clear our the remnant of the red guys, and do it all over again. And again. And again.Oh, and the way they staggered gear progression is another major issue. Crafting is hardgated behind the armory building in your base and you need to claim an iron mine to build that. And because I didn't find an iron mine until like hour 7 of play, a lot of my looted gear was equivalent or better than the crafted gear. I was only able to start crafting gear after 7-hours! Couple that with the lack of mid-game story progression, mediocre base building system, wonky time-progression system, and a stale gameplay loop and you have a recipe for disappointment. Party management becomes a nuisance. Party combat becomes a nuisance. Army battles become a nuisance. Traveling from area to area becomes a nuisance. So you exit the game and never go back again.If you feel like you have the patience to continuously play the exact same little loop over and over again, then this might be a decent game for you. Otherwise, just move on.

I love LEGO, I love all sorts of racing games, and have played thousands of hours of them. However, for LEGO 2K DRIVE, 2K tried to take both roads with the pricing model and ended up turning a lot of people away. You either make a game that's $60 with **NO** MICROTRANSACTIONS, or you make a game free-to-play with microtransactions that are cosmetic at most. As they say, you can't have your cake and eat it too.The game itself is a true blast, it's got a lot going for it. It's like a mix between Forza Horizon and The Crew 2's open world, with the Lego Racers aesthetic, aimed at a younger demographic. The game's story is quite fun for me so far and its car editor/builder is a huge time-waster that works surprisingly well on a controller. It's got a good open world that's fun to explore, it's not as big as I expected it would be but it's big enough to be worthwhile to just drive around in finding collectibles and destroying everything. The big thing holding that aspect back is that they developed this for last-gen consoles (notably Switch) so instead of it being a true, seamless open-world, it's five worlds that are each an area/biome. That's fine, but it makes me wonder what that aspect of the game could've been if it were a seamless open world.However, for a game aimed at kids, the microtransactions & in-game shop in this game are quite predatory. It takes quite some time to be able to buy ONE vehicle, and honestly you should be able to buy your first microtransaction vehicle by a couple of hours into the game, not take about 20 hours to get a ton of BrikBux before buying your first vehicle. The grind itself doesn't bother me personally, I play a lot of games with it. However, the intention of 2K and Visual Concepts is to make you get frustrated enough while playing the game to just give in and spend more money on a car instead of spending time unlocking it. That is by design, especially as this game is built for and marketed towards children, who naturally have less patience than adults.In conclusion, the gameplay itself is fun but the business model from 2K and Visual Concepts is not. I'd say I expected better, but in 2023 that would be a lie. It hurts me to not recommend this title because the core gameplay is there, but I cannot in good faith recommend it because of the way its business model preys on children. If you want to buy it, wait until it is on a deep sale, which will probably be pretty quick based on what I have seen of previous 2K first-party titles. At the same time, only buy it and go in knowing that you will be spammed by menus asking you to buy microtransactions, so avoid them at all costs.PARENTS: DO NOT BUY THIS GAME FOR YOUR KIDS. However, if you feel so strongly that you have to, PLEASE stay in the room with them and supervise them while playing it. THIS GAME'S IN-GAME STORE IS AIMED AT CHILDREN, and they WILL fall for it if they are not careful. I hate that I have to say something like this for a video game, especially one based off of such a fun pastime such as LEGOs, but 2K has forced my hand to have to say something like this.EDIT 05/30/2023: Just when I thought 2K could not stoop any lower, they do just that. In a recent patch, they fixed a crash that happened when going into Unkie's Emporium. That's the only thing they did. The catch? That's where the cosmetics and microtransaction shop is. The fact that they found it necessary to release an update to fix that and only that in a fully-priced game should tell you all you need to know about 2K and Visual Concepts.

Like the devs say it really brings all the diversity of the Warhammer world to life in one chaotic and cataclysmic campaign. In my opinion, it's quite frankly pathetic, especially for an £80 game.Added note: WHY THE F**K CAN'T YOU TAB-OUT IN GAME?

I have enjoyed my time playing this game and figuring out how things work. I do hope that it becomes something great with how the combat is and quests go. However, as with the current build of a pre-alpha, I do not recommend this game at the current price. I understand that they promise to put in all the effort they can and you'll receive every update that comes around over time. However, they should of put it up on Steam for 20 dollars. I think that would have been reasonable instead of the big 30. But if you have good faith on the devs and want to support then you can support them on their Patreon.As you should know, the game itself in the current state is the most bare bones it can be. So if I do get this, be sure to check it after a year or six months for more real content.
